title: The Greek alphabet and its sounds
intro: The 24 letters, then the small marks and letter pairs that change how a word sounds. Sounds follow the Erasmian pronunciation the lessons use; the Restored Koine sound (closer to the first century) is shown beside it. Tap a letter for more, and Listen to hear an example.

letters.name: gamma
letters.sound: g as in go; ng before γ κ χ ξ
letters.koine: a soft g; like y before e and i sounds
letters.tip: It looks a little like y, but it is g.

letters.name: eta
letters.koine: e as in met, held a little longer
letters.tip: It looks like an English n, but it is a vowel.

letters.name: theta
letters.tip: One letter for one sound: th.

letters.name: iota
letters.sound: ee as in machine; i as in sit in a closed syllable
letters.tip: No dot on top. Written small under α, η or ω it is silent (ᾳ ῃ ῳ).

letters.name: nu
letters.tip: It looks like an English v, but it is n.

letters.name: xi
letters.tip: One letter for two sounds, k + s.

letters.name: rho
letters.tip: It looks like an English p, but it is r. At the start of a word it carries a rough breathing (ῥ), which isn't said.

letters.name: sigma
letters.sound: s; ς at the end of a word
letters.koine: s; z before β γ δ μ
letters.tip: Two small forms: σ at the start or in the middle, ς at the very end. πίστις has both.

letters.name: upsilon
letters.sound: ü as in French tu (or simply oo)
letters.tip: At the start of a word it always has a rough breathing: hü-.

letters.name: chi
letters.tip: It looks like an English x, but it is kh.

letters.name: psi
letters.tip: One letter for two sounds, p + s.

letters.name: omega
letters.koine: o as in lot (the same as ο)
letters.tip: “Big o”. It looks like an English w, but it is a vowel.

sections.title: Marks that change the sound
body: A rough breathing ῾ over the first vowel adds an h; a smooth breathing ᾿ adds nothing. With a pair of vowels the mark sits on the second: οὐρανός, υἱός.
The accent (´ ` or ῀) shows which syllable to stress. In the Erasmian pronunciation all three just mean “stress here”.
A small ι under α, η or ω (ᾳ ῃ ῳ) is silent. Two dots over a vowel (¨) mean it is said on its own, not as part of a pair.
γ before γ, κ, χ or ξ is said ng: ἄγγελος is ANG-ge-los.

examples.en: the mark sits on the second vowel: son
stress where the accent is: person
the little ι is silent: beginning
¨ keeps α and ι apart: Isaiah

sections.title: Pairs of vowels
body: These pairs are said as one sound. In the first century several of them had already moved towards other sounds, shown on the right.

sections.title: Erasmian and Restored Koine
body: Erasmian, taught in most colleges, gives every letter its own sound, which helps with spelling. Restored Koine aims at how Greek sounded in the first century: closer to Modern Greek, with fewer distinct vowels. Choose which one the Listen buttons use in Settings.

sections.title: Punctuation and signs in the text
body: Full stops and commas work as in English. A raised dot · is a pause like a colon or semicolon, and often comes just before someone's words. ; is the Greek question mark.
An apostrophe shows a dropped vowel before another vowel: δι’ αὐτοῦ is διά αὐτοῦ, “through him”. Capitals mark names and the start of a paragraph, not every sentence.

Double brackets ⟦ ⟧ (shown [[ ]] in the Reader) mark passages that most scholars think were added after the Gospel was first written, such as John 7:53–8:11 and Mark 16:9–20. The Reader explains them where they appear.

The printed NA28 also has a list of manuscript readings at the foot of each page (the apparatus), with its own signs. That isn't part of this app, and none of it changes how the main text is read aloud.

practice.en: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.
For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son…
